question: What is the purpose of @BeforeEach and @AfterEach in JUnit 5?
title: @BeforeEach @AfterEach JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: @BeforeEach runs a setup method before every single test. @AfterEach runs a cleanup method after every test. They ensure each test starts with a fresh, known state — preventing tests from accidentally sharing state and causing flaky failures.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of test isolation and setup/teardown lifecycle in JUnit 5
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a single shared instance across all tests causing tests to affect each other
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why fresh instances are critical for test independence and connect to the FIRST principles (Fast, Independent, Repeatable, Self-validating, Timely)

sections.title: Setup and Teardown for Every Test
sections.content: **@BeforeEach** and **@AfterEach** are lifecycle annotations that control what happens around each test method. Think of them like a factory reset button — @BeforeEach builds a clean environment before every test runs, and @AfterEach tears it down afterward. This ensures **test isolation**: each test gets its own fresh objects, so tests can't accidentally share state. Without this, one test might modify a shared list or database connection, causing the next test to fail unpredictably. In production testing, you'll use @BeforeEach to initialize mocks, create test data, or open database connections, and @AfterEach to close resources or reset static state. This pattern is crucial for the **Independent** principle in FIRST — tests must run in any order without affecting each other.

rows: Test won't run if setup fails

sections.title: Using @BeforeEach and @AfterEach in a Service Test
Key Points
content: **@BeforeEach**: Runs before every test method in the class, creating fresh test fixtures each time
**@AfterEach**: Runs after every test method completes, used for cleanup and resource closure
**Test Isolation**: Each test gets its own setup, preventing one test from polluting another's state
**Inheritance**: Setup methods in parent test classes run before child class setups, teardown runs in reverse order
**Failure Handling**: If @BeforeEach fails, the test is marked as failed and won't execute; @AfterEach always runs if setup succeeded
**Resource Management**: Use @AfterEach to close database connections, file handles, or reset static fields
**FIRST Principles**: These annotations enforce the Independent principle — tests must not depend on execution order

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: At-BeforeEach runs a setup method before every single test in the class. At-AfterEach runs a cleanup method after each test finishes. They're lifecycle hooks that ensure every test starts with a fresh, known state. For example, if you're testing an OrderService, you'd use at-BeforeEach to create a new service instance and a clean list of test orders. Without it, one test might add items to the list, and the next test would see those leftover items, causing unpredictable failures. That's called a flaky test. After the test, at-AfterEach clears the list and nulls out references so memory can be freed. This pattern enforces test isolation, which is the I in FIRST principles. Each test is Independent and can run in any order. A common mistake freshers make is creating shared objects at the class level and reusing them across tests. That breaks isolation. If one test modifies a shared list, the next test sees the modified version, and suddenly your tests fail randomly depending on execution order. Always use at-BeforeEach to create fresh instances. In real projects with Spring Boot, you'd also use it to initialize Mockito mocks or reset database state before each test runs.

question: What does @DisplayName do in JUnit 5 and why should you use it?
title: @DisplayName JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: @DisplayName provides a human-readable name for a test class or method that appears in test reports and IDE output. It lets you write descriptive sentences like 'should return zero tax when salary is below threshold' instead of method names like testTaxCalcBelowThreshold.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of JUnit 5 improvements over JUnit 4 and focus on test readability
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing cryptic test method names like test1, test2 which are useless in failure reports
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a realistic @DisplayName example and explain how it makes CI reports readable for non-developers like product managers or QA

sections.title: Human-Readable Test Names
sections.content: **@DisplayName** is a JUnit 5 annotation that replaces the method name with a readable label in test reports and IDE test runners. In JUnit 4, you were stuck with Java method naming rules: camelCase, no spaces, no special characters. So tests ended up named like `testCalculateTaxWhenSalaryBelowThreshold` — hard to read in a CI failure email. @DisplayName lets you write natural language: `"should return zero tax when salary is below threshold"`. This makes test reports readable for **everyone** on the team — not just developers. When a CI pipeline fails and sends a report to Slack, product managers and QA engineers can understand which business scenario broke without decoding camelCase. The annotation works on both test methods and test classes, letting you create a full hierarchy of readable names. This is one of JUnit 5's major quality-of-life improvements.

sections.title: Using @DisplayName for Readable Test Reports
Key Points
content: **@DisplayName**: Annotation that provides a human-readable label for test classes and methods in reports
**Natural Language**: Supports spaces, punctuation, and emojis — write tests as readable sentences
**CI/CD Reports**: Failed tests show the display name in Jenkins, GitLab CI, or GitHub Actions output
**IDE Integration**: IntelliJ IDEA and Eclipse show display names in the test runner panel
**Class and Method**: Can be applied to both test classes and individual test methods for full hierarchy
**JUnit 4 Difference**: JUnit 4 had no equivalent — you were stuck with method names or third-party runners
**Team Communication**: Makes test failures understandable for non-developers reviewing CI reports

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: At-DisplayName provides a human-readable name for a test that shows up in test reports and your IDE. Instead of writing method names like testTaxCalcBelowThreshold, you can write a full sentence: should return zero tax when salary is below threshold. This makes test reports way more readable, especially for people who aren't developers. If a test fails in your CI pipeline and sends a Slack notification, the product manager can read should apply twenty percent tax rate when salary is between fifty-k and hundred-k and immediately understand what broke. They don't have to decode camelCase method names. You can use it on both test classes and test methods. Put it on the class to label the whole suite, like Tax Calculator Service, and on methods for individual scenarios. The annotation accepts any string, including spaces and punctuation. A common mistake freshers make is writing useless method names like test1, test2, or just test. When that test fails in production, nobody knows what it was testing. Always use descriptive names. At-DisplayName takes this a step further by letting you write plain English. It's a JUnit 5 feature, so it didn't exist in JUnit 4. This is one of the big improvements that makes JUnit 5 much better for team collaboration.

question: What is @Disabled in JUnit 5 and when should you use it?
title: @Disabled JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: @Disabled skips a test method or class, marking it as ignored in test reports. Use it when a test is known to fail due to a bug being tracked, when a feature is not yet implemented, or temporarily during development — always with a reason string explaining why.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical testing knowledge and the right way to skip tests instead of deleting them
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Commenting out tests instead of using @Disabled which makes tests disappear from reports
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note that @Disabled tests show up as skipped in reports, which is visible and trackable, unlike commented tests that are invisible

sections.title: Skipping Tests with Visibility
sections.content: **@Disabled** tells JUnit 5 to skip a test method or entire test class without deleting the code. The test won't run, but it appears in test reports marked as **skipped** with your reason message. This is the correct way to temporarily disable tests — not commenting them out. Use @Disabled when you're tracking a known bug ("Disabled until API-4523 is fixed"), when a feature isn't implemented yet ("Disabled — payment gateway integration pending"), or during active development. The key benefit is **visibility**: CI reports show 47 passed, 3 skipped, making disabled tests trackable. If you comment out a test, it disappears from the codebase's test count, and people forget it exists. Then months later, someone discovers a critical scenario was never tested. Always include a reason string in @Disabled so future developers understand why the test is off. Think of it like a TODO that's visible in every test run.

sections.title: Using @Disabled to Skip Tests with Context
Key Points
content: **@Disabled**: Annotation that skips a test method or class, marking it as ignored in test reports
**Reason String**: Always include a message explaining why the test is disabled and when it should be re-enabled
**Report Visibility**: Disabled tests show as skipped in CI reports, unlike commented tests that disappear
**Use Cases**: Known bugs being tracked, unimplemented features, flaky tests being investigated, or temporary development work
**Class Level**: Can disable an entire test class by putting @Disabled on the class declaration
**JUnit 4 Equivalent**: Replaces @Ignore from JUnit 4, which had the same purpose but different name
**Tracking**: Makes it easy to search the codebase for all disabled tests and review why they're off

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: At-Disabled skips a test method or class without running it. The test shows up as skipped in your test reports, not as a failure or success. You should use it when a test is failing due to a known bug that's being tracked, or when a feature isn't implemented yet. Always include a reason string explaining why it's disabled. For example, at-Disabled with the message Disabled until Stripe webhook integration is complete, ticket JIRA-1234. This tells future developers exactly why the test is off and when to turn it back on. The big advantage over commenting out the test is visibility. If you comment out a test, it completely disappears from your test suite. Nobody sees it in reports. Six months later, someone realizes a critical payment scenario was never tested because the test was commented out and forgotten. With at-Disabled, your CI report shows something like forty-seven passed, three skipped. You can search your codebase for at-Disabled and review all skipped tests. A common mistake is commenting out flaky or failing tests to make the build green. Don't do that. Use at-Disabled with a reason, and create a ticket to fix it. In JUnit 4, the equivalent was at-Ignore. JUnit 5 renamed it to at-Disabled, which is more explicit about what it does.

question: What is @ExtendWith in JUnit 5 and when do you use it?
title: @ExtendWith JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: @ExtendWith registers an extension that adds behavior to the test lifecycle — like integrating Mockito or Spring. @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) enables @Mock and @InjectMocks annotations automatically. It replaces JUnit 4's @RunWith.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know how to integrate Mockito or Spring with JUnit 5 using the extension model
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using MockitoAnnotations.openMocks(this) in @BeforeEach instead of the cleaner @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @ExtendWith replaced @RunWith from JUnit 4, and that @SpringBootTest implicitly includes @ExtendWith(SpringExtension.class)

sections.title: Extending JUnit 5 with Custom Behavior
sections.content: **@ExtendWith** is JUnit 5's mechanism for plugging in extensions that modify test behavior. An **extension** is a class that hooks into the test lifecycle — like running code before tests start, initializing objects, or cleaning up resources. The most common use case for freshers is **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)**, which enables Mockito's @Mock and @InjectMocks annotations. Without this extension, those annotations don't work — you'd have to manually call MockitoAnnotations.openMocks(this) in @BeforeEach, which is verbose and error-prone. Another frequent use is **@ExtendWith(SpringExtension.class)**, which integrates the Spring container with JUnit. However, if you use @SpringBootTest, that annotation already includes SpringExtension, so you don't add it manually. @ExtendWith replaces JUnit 4's @RunWith, which only allowed one runner at a time. JUnit 5 lets you stack multiple @ExtendWith annotations, making it far more flexible.

sections.title: Using @ExtendWith with Mockito for Dependency Injection
Key Points
content: **@ExtendWith**: Registers an extension class that adds custom behavior to the JUnit 5 test lifecycle
**MockitoExtension**: The most common extension for freshers, enables @Mock and @InjectMocks annotations automatically
**SpringExtension**: Integrates Spring's dependency injection container with JUnit 5 for integration tests
**Replaces @RunWith**: JUnit 4 used @RunWith(SpringRunner.class) — JUnit 5 uses @ExtendWith(SpringExtension.class)
**Multiple Extensions**: You can stack multiple @ExtendWith annotations, unlike JUnit 4's single-runner limitation
**Implicit Extensions**: @SpringBootTest already includes SpringExtension, so you don't add it manually
**Manual Alternative**: Without @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class), you'd call MockitoAnnotations.openMocks(this) in @BeforeEach

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: At-ExtendWith registers an extension that adds behavior to the test lifecycle. An extension is like a plugin that hooks into JUnit and provides extra features. The most common one you'll see is at-ExtendWith with MockitoExtension dot class. This enables Mockito's at-Mock and at-InjectMocks annotations. Without this extension, those annotations don't do anything. You'd have to manually initialize mocks by calling MockitoAnnotations dot openMocks in a before-each method, which is messy. With the extension, Mockito automatically creates the mocks before each test runs. Another common extension is SpringExtension, which integrates Spring's dependency injection container with JUnit. However, if you're using at-SpringBootTest, that annotation already includes SpringExtension under the hood, so you don't need to add it yourself. At-ExtendWith replaced at-RunWith from JUnit 4. In JUnit 4, you'd write at-RunWith with SpringRunner dot class or MockitoJUnitRunner dot class. JUnit 5 unified this into the extension model. The big improvement is you can stack multiple at-ExtendWith annotations on one test class, while JUnit 4 only allowed one runner. For example, you could combine Mockito and a custom database extension. A common mistake is forgetting to add at-ExtendWith when using at-Mock, then wondering why the mocks are null. Always include MockitoExtension when using Mockito annotations.

question: What is @Nested in JUnit 5 and how does it improve test organization?
title: @Nested Tests JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: @Nested allows inner test classes that group related tests together, creating a hierarchy. Outer class can contain @BeforeEach that applies to nested tests. It produces a readable tree structure in IDEs and CI reports showing test organization by scenario or method.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of JUnit 5's organizational features and ability to structure large test suites
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Having a flat list of 30 test methods in one class without any logical grouping — @Nested provides structure without separate test files
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show how @Nested combined with @DisplayName creates a test tree that reads like a specification document or BDD scenarios

sections.title: Hierarchical Test Organization
sections.content: **@Nested** lets you create inner test classes inside a main test class, forming a **test hierarchy**. Think of it like organizing files into folders — instead of 30 test methods in a flat list, you group them logically: "Valid Input Tests", "Error Handling Tests", "Edge Cases". Each nested class can have its own @BeforeEach setup that runs in addition to the outer class setup. This avoids duplication when different test groups need different initialization. The big payoff is **readability**: your IDE and CI reports show a tree structure like a table of contents. Combined with @DisplayName, nested tests read like a **specification document** or BDD scenarios. For example, the tree might show "UserService → Registration → should reject duplicate email → should accept valid email format". This is far clearer than 30 methods named testRegistration1, testRegistration2. It's especially useful when testing a class with multiple methods — nest tests by method name.

sections.title: Using @Nested to Group Related Tests
Key Points
content: **@Nested**: Annotation for inner test classes that creates a hierarchical test structure in reports
**Logical Grouping**: Organize tests by feature, method, or scenario instead of a flat list of methods
**Inherited Setup**: Nested classes inherit @BeforeEach and @BeforeAll from the outer class, avoiding duplication
**Additional Setup**: Nested classes can add their own @BeforeEach that runs after the outer setup
**IDE Tree View**: Test runners display nested tests as an expandable tree structure
**Combined with @DisplayName**: Creates readable test documentation that looks like a specification
**No JUnit 4 Equivalent**: This is a JUnit 5-only feature — JUnit 4 had no native support for test hierarchies

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: At-Nested allows you to create inner test classes that group related tests together. Instead of having thirty test methods in a flat list, you can organize them into logical sections. For example, if you're testing a UserService with registration, login, and password reset methods, you'd create three nested classes, one for each feature. Each nested class is marked with at-Nested and can have its own at-DisplayName. The outer class can have a before-each setup that runs for all tests, and nested classes can add their own before-each that runs afterward. This avoids duplicating setup code. The real benefit is readability. In your IDE or CI reports, you see a tree structure. The root is User Registration Service, with branches for Email Validation and Password Strength, and individual tests under each branch. Combined with at-DisplayName, it reads like documentation: should reject duplicate email addresses, should require at least eight characters. This is way better than seeing testRegistration1, testRegistration2 in a flat list. A common mistake is putting all tests in one class with no organization. When you have thirty methods, it's hard to find the one that failed. At-Nested gives you structure without creating separate test files for every scenario. It's a JUnit 5-only feature. JUnit 4 didn't have this, so you'd either make separate test classes or use naming prefixes like testLogin underscore validCredentials. At-Nested is much cleaner.
